title: The services page a fintech product actually needs
metaTitle: The fintech product services page buyers can use
excerpt: List each fintech service in the buyer's words, with the outcome, the boundary, and a next step to open an account or talk to sales.
alt: Speckled ceramic cups and a two-tone vase arranged on a white shelf, a small set of distinct objects for a page that should list distinct services.
caption: Cups and a vase on a white shelf. Each service should be this easy to tell apart. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: How is a services page different from a feature list?
faqs.answer: A feature list names capabilities. A services page names the job a buyer can hire you for, what they get, and what you will not take on. "Real-time ledger" is a feature, while a line about recording every payout for a finance lead is a service. The page should be written as jobs.

faqs.question: How many services should a fintech site list?
faqs.answer: List the jobs you want a stranger to buy, not every internal workstream. Three to six clear services are usually enough for a first serious page. A grid of twenty vague capabilities forces the buyer to invent the offer. If two services always sell together, write them as one offer with a boundary.

faqs.question: Where should the next step sit on a services page?
faqs.answer: On each service, not only in the header. The next step is to start an account or talk to sales, and the label should say which buyer that service is for. A single "Contact" button at the bottom of a long grid makes every service feel equally unfinished.

sources.title: Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
A fintech product services page should list the work in the buyer's language. For someone who may trust you with money, each service needs an outcome, a boundary, and a next step: start an account, or talk to sales.

A grid of vague capabilities does not help. "Platform," "infrastructure," and "solutions" are how a team describes itself in a meeting. A buyer is trying to match a job they already have to something you will actually do.

## Name the job, not the department

Start from the sentence the buyer would use with a colleague. "We need payouts to sellers in three countries." "We need a card our contractors can use without a shared login." "We need a ledger our accountant will accept." Those sentences are the services. Your internal names can sit in a smaller line if a returning customer searches for them.

Google's guidance on title links asks for titles that are descriptive and concise, and for a page that makes the main subject obvious. The same standard belongs on each service heading. "Global money movement" is not a subject. "Payouts to sellers" is. A heading should be something a person could repeat after one reading, and something you would be willing to see as the title of that section in a search result.

Give each service its own block, with room for three short parts. Do not collapse the page into icons. Icons can support a label. They cannot carry the boundary. If the service cannot be explained without a diagram of your whole platform, it is not a service yet. It is the platform, and it belongs on the homepage as the product.

A services page still needs a primary purpose. Google's people-first questions ask whether the site, and by extension the page, has a focus a visitor can name. "Everything we are able to do" is not a focus. "The jobs you can hire this product to do" is.

## Write the outcome in one sentence

The outcome is the change in the buyer's week, not the technology you are proud of. "Sellers get paid without your team uploading a file" is an outcome. "API-first payout orchestration" is a method. Lead with the outcome. Put the method in the next sentence if it helps a technical buyer trust the outcome.

Keep the sentence specific enough to exclude someone. A line that could sit on any fintech homepage is a line that has not chosen a buyer. Mention the person who feels the change. A finance lead. An operator. A marketplace founder. A clinic manager is the wrong room. Stay with the person who moves the money.

One outcome per service. If you need three sentences of outcomes, you are describing three services, or you are describing a platform. Split them or cut them. A buyer scanning the page should be able to stop on the block that matches the job and ignore the rest without feeling they missed a trick.

Trade Moai, a public Hanabi project, is organized so a person can scan. The lesson transfers. A services page is a scan, then a choice. Equal visual weight on twelve outcomes means there is no choice, only a poster.

## State the boundary in the same block

The boundary is what you will not do inside this service. It is the part teams skip because it feels like lost revenue. It is the part a money buyer uses to decide you are safe to talk to.

Boundaries that belong on a fintech services page:

- Countries or currencies you do not support in this offer.
- Whether you hold funds or a partner does.
- Whether the buyer must already have an entity, a bank, or a license.
- What your team does, and what remains their engineers' work.
- The volume or risk level that moves the buyer from self-serve to a conversation.

Write the boundary as a fact. "This payout service does not include card issuing" is clear. "Additional modules available" is a doorway back into vagueness. If a related service exists, link it by the job name. Do not make the reader guess which icon is the cousin of this one.

A boundary also protects your team. The page becomes the thing sales and delivery can both point at. When a prospect asks for cash handling and the page says you do not do that, the conversation stays short and honest. That is a better outcome than a services grid that seemed to promise everything.

## Put the next step on the service, not only in the header

Each block ends with the action that fits that service. Some services are something a person can start: open an account, submit the entity, connect a bank. Some are a conversation: talk to sales, with a line about what to have ready. Volume, entities, and the job in their words.

Do not send every block to the same unlabeled "Learn more." If the deeper page exists, the link text should name it. "Read how payouts settle" is a next step. "Learn more" is a stall. If there is no deeper page, do not pretend. The account button or the sales button is the next step.

Match the verb to the risk. Opening an account is a serious action. The button can say so. "Start application" is clearer than "Get started" when the next screen asks for a tax identity. Talking to sales is also serious. "Book a fit call" is clearer than "Request a demo" if you will spend the time on scope, not on a feature tour.

Repeat the action in the same words at the bottom of the page for the person who scanned and is ready. One repeated path. Not a new menu of whitepapers, webinars, and a chatbot that asks them to restate the service they already chose.

## How many services, and in what order

Order the page by the jobs you most want a stranger to recognize, not by the age of the product line. The first service should be the one a careful buyer can verify against the homepage. If the homepage is about payouts, payouts should not be the fourth card.

Three services you can explain beat eight you cannot. A young product often has one real service and a list of intentions. Publish the real one. Put intentions on a roadmap page if customers ask, or leave them off the site until a buyer can purchase them. A services page full of "coming soon" trains people to doubt the lines that are ready.

When two offers differ only by a limit, they are one service with a boundary, not two departments. "Payouts" and "Payouts plus" can be a pricing distinction. They do not both need a services block unless the job itself changes. The test is whether a buyer could hire one and not the other and still describe different work.

Use the buyer's sequence, not your onboarding sequence. They do not care that compliance review happens in week two of your internal checklist. They care whether this service includes that review or expects them to bring an approval you will not provide. Say which.

## Proof next to the service it supports

A logo row under the whole grid does not prove any single service. If you have a story, attach it to the service it illustrates. One constraint, one decision, one result you can say in a sentence. "A marketplace needed seller payouts without a weekly file. We settled to their existing bank rails and left card issuing out." That is proof. A screenshot of a dashboard with no decision is decoration.

If you cannot name the customer, describe the situation without pretending it is a case study. "Teams with this shape use this service" is allowed when it is true. "Trusted by leading brands" is not a situation. Google's expertise questions are a fair bar here. Trust comes from evidence a reader can inspect, including who is speaking. A service block with no owner and no example asks the reader to supply both.

Hanabi's selected work is a public record of product and site decisions, not a wall of unnamed marks. [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works) is the place to see how a studio frames a real constraint, which is the same discipline a services page needs from you.

## A review pass before you publish the grid

Read every heading and cover the body. Could a stranger say what they would get? If the headings only make sense after the paragraph, rename them. Then read every boundary and ask whether sales would be relieved or annoyed to see it in public. Relief means it belongs. Annoyance often means the page is telling the truth the pitch has been softening.

Check the verbs against the homepage and the pricing page. The same job should have the same name in all three places. A buyer who saw "payouts" on the homepage should not meet "disbursements" here and "transfers" on pricing unless you explain the difference in one clause. Synonyms feel like writing. They feel like three products.

Finally, open the page on a phone and tap only the service you would buy if you were the buyer. Count the taps to a real next step. If the answer is a general contact form that does not know which service you chose, the page has not finished. Pass the service name into the conversation. Make the person on the other side start from the job, not from "how can we help."

The page after this one is about the people, not the menu. [How a fintech product should write an about page](/blog/how-a-fintech-product-should-write-an-about-page) covers who to name, and which origin stories are worth the space.
